{{Short description|Scrolls from ancient Italy}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=February 2024}}

[[File:Herculaneum papyri.jpg|thumb|Papyrus fragments PHerc.1103 (a) and PHerc.110 (b,c). Image contrast and brightness were enhanced to better visualize the details visible to the naked eye on their external surface.<ref name="nature2021">{{cite journal |last1=Stabile |first1=Sara |last2=Palermo |first2=Francesca |last3=Bukreeva |first3=Inna |last4=Mele |first4=Daniela |last5=Formoso |first5=Vincenzo |last6=Bartolino |first6=Roberto |last7=Cedola |first7=Alessia |title=A computational platform for the virtual unfolding of Herculaneum Papyri |journal=Scientific Reports |date=18 January 2021 |volume=11 |issue=1 |page=1695 |doi=10.1038/s41598-020-80458-z  |doi-access=free|pmid=33462265 |pmc=7813886 |bibcode=2021NatSR..11.1695S }}</ref>]]
The '''Herculaneum papyri''' are more than 1,800 [[scroll]]s of [[papyrus]] discovered in the 18th century in the [[Villa of the Papyri]] in [[Herculaneum]]. They had been [[Carbonization|carbonized]] when the villa was engulfed by the [[eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 AD]]. 

The papyri, containing a number of [[Greek Philosophy|Greek philosophical texts]], come from the only surviving [[library]] from antiquity that exists in its entirety.<ref name="napoleon1">[http://www.napoleon.org/en/magazine/interviews/files/476891.asp#informations Interview with Daniel Delattre: The Herculaneum scrolls given to Consul Bonaparte (2010), Napoleon.org] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151030232207/http://www.napoleon.org/en/magazine/interviews/files/476891.asp |date=2015-10-30}}</ref> In its current state, reading of the scrolls is extremely difficult and can risk destroying the information it holds. Techniques to decipher the writings on the scrolls are still being developed. For the first time, researchers recovered all the surviving text from a single scroll in 2026.<ref>{{cite web |title=Scientists Have Deciphered the Surviving Fragments of a 2,000-Year-Old Philosophical Treatise Frozen in Time by Mount Vesuvius' Eruption |website=Smithsonian Magazine |author=Ellen Wexler |date=June 26, 2026 |url=https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/scientists-have-deciphered-the-surviving-fragments-of-a-2000-year-old-philosophical-treatise-frozen-in-time-by-mount-vesuvius-eruption-180989036/ |access-date=22 October 2026}}</ref><ref name="Angelotti2026">{{cite arXiv |eprint=2606.29085 |title=Complete virtual unwrapping and reading of a rolled Herculaneum papyrus |author1=Giorgio Angelotti |author2=Stephen Parsons |author3=Federica Nicolardi |author4=Youssef Nader |author5=W. Brent Seales |date=27 June 2026 |class=eess.IV}}</ref>

The majority of classical texts referred to by other classical authors are lost, and there is hope that the continuing work on the library scrolls will discover some of these. For example, as many as 44 works discovered were written by the 1st-century BC [[Epicureanism|Epicurean]] philosopher and poet [[Philodemus]], a resident of Herculaneum, who possibly formed the library, or whose library was incorporated in it.

==Discovery==
[[File:Dionysus-or-Plato-Herculaneum-papyri-Villa-of-the-Papyri-Barker.jpg|thumb|[[Dionysus]], [[Plato]], or [[Poseidon]] sculpture excavated at the Villa of the Papyri]]
[[File:Herculaneum,_past,_present_and_future_(1908)_(14596218878).jpg|thumb|A map of the [[Villa of the Papyri]]]]
Due to the eruption of [[Mount Vesuvius]] in 79 AD, bundles of scrolls were carbonized by the intense heat of the [[pyroclastic flow]]s.<ref name="smithsonianmag.com"/> This intense parching took place over an extremely short period of time, in a room deprived of oxygen, resulting in the scrolls' carbonization into compact and highly fragile blocks.<ref name="napoleon1"/> They were then preserved by the layers of cement-like rock.<ref name="smithsonianmag.com"/>

In 1752, workmen of the [[House of Bourbon|Bourbon royal family]] accidentally discovered what is now known as the [[Villa of the Papyri]].<ref name="napoleon1"/><ref name="diringer">{{Cite book |last=Diringer |first=David |author-link=David Diringer |title=The Book Before Printing: Ancient, Medieval and Oriental |publisher=Dover Publications |place=New York |year=1982 |url=https://archive.org/details/bookbeforeprinti0000diri/page/252 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/bookbeforeprinti0000diri/page/252 252–6] |isbn=978-0-486-24243-9 }}</ref> There may still be a lower section of the Villa's collection that remains buried.<ref name="smithsonianmag.com">{{cite web|last=Jaggard|first=Victoria|url=https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/ancient-scrolls-blackened-vesuvius-are-readable-last-herculaneum-papyri-180953950/|title=Ancient Scrolls Blackened by Vesuvius Are Readable at Last|work=[[Smithsonian (magazine)|Smithsonian]]|date=20 January 2015|access-date=15 January 2025}}</ref>

Ethel Ross Barker noted in her 1908 ''Buried Herculaneum'':<ref name="Barker">{{cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/buriedherculaneu00barkuoft|title=Buried Herculaneum|author=Ethel Ross Barker|year=1908|publisher=London : A. & C. Black}}</ref>
{{Quote|Appearance of the rolls. — A large number of papyri, after being buried eighteen centuries, have been found in the Villa named after them. In appearance the rolls resembled lumps of charcoal; and many were thrown away as such. Some were much lighter in colour. Finally, a faint trace of letters was seen on one of the blackened masses, which was found to be a roll of papyrus, disintegrated by decay and damp, full of holes, cut, crushed, and crumpled. The papyri were found at a depth of about {{convert|120|ft|m|abbr=off}}.

The woodwork of some of the [[Bookcase|press]]es that had contained them dropped to dust on exposure and many rolls were found lying about loosely. Others were still on the shelves. Locality of the discovery. — They were found in four places on four occasions. The first were found in the autumn of 1752, fourteen years after the first discovery of Herculaneum, in and near the [[tablinum]], and only numbered some 21 volumes and fragments, contained in two wooden cases. In the spring of 1753, 11 papyri were found in a room just south of the tablinum, and in the summer of the same year, 250 were found in a room to the north. In the spring and summer of the following year, 337 Greek papyri and 18 Latin papyri were found in the Library. Nothing of any importance was discovered after this date.

The numbers given here exclude mere fragments. Including every tiny fragment found, the catalogues give 1756 manuscripts discovered up to 1855, while subsequent discoveries bring the total up to 1806. Of these, 341 were found almost entire, 500 were merely charred fragments, and the remaining 965 were in every intermediate state of disintegration.

Treatment of the rolls. — No one knew how to deal with such strange material. Weber, the engineer, and Paderni, the keeper of the Museum at Portici, were not experts in [[palaeography]] and [[philology]], which sciences were, indeed, almost in their infancy one hundred and fifty years ago. There were no official publications concerning the papyri till forty years after their discovery, and our information is of necessity incomplete, inexact and contradictory.

Father [[Antonio Piaggio]]'s machine. — Through this inevitable ignorance of the time, a larger number of the rolls were destroyed than the difficulties of the case necessitated. Many had been thrown away as mere charcoal; some were destroyed in extracting them from the lava in which they were embedded. In the attempt to discover their contents, several were split in two longitudinally. Finally, that ingenious Italian monk, Father Piaggio, invented a very simple machine for unrolling the manuscripts by means of silk threads attached to the edge of the papyrus. Of course this method destroyed the beginning of all the papyri, sometimes the end could not be found, and the papyri were in a terrible state of decay.}}

===Excavations===
{{quote|text=Anybody who focuses on the ancient world is always going to be excited to get even one paragraph, one chapter, more... The prospect of getting hundreds of books more is staggering.<br>Roger Macfarlane<ref name="smithsonianmag.com"/>}}

In the 18th century, the first digs began. The excavation appeared closer to mining projects, as mineshafts were dug, and horizontal subterranean galleries were installed. Workers would place objects in baskets and send them back up.<ref name="napoleon1"/>

With the backing of [[Charles III of Spain|Charles VII of Naples]] (1716–1788), [[Roque Joaquín de Alcubierre]] headed the systematic excavation of Herculaneum with [[Karl Jakob Weber]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://sites.google.com/site/ad79eruption/dramatis-personae/since-the-re-discovery|title=Since the Re-discovery - AD79eruption|work=google.com|access-date=2015-09-08|archive-date=2015-11-25|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151125111806/https://sites.google.com/site/ad79eruption/dramatis-personae/since-the-re-discovery}}</ref>

Barker noted in her 1908 ''Buried Herculaneum'', "By the orders of [[Francis I of the Two Sicilies|Francis I]] land was purchased, and in 1828 excavations were begun in two parts {{convert|150|ft|m|disp=sqbr}} apart, under the direction of the architect. Carlo Bonucci. In the year 1868 still further purchases of land were made, and excavations were carried on in an eastward direction till 1875. The total area now open measures 300 by 150 perches (1510 by 756 meters). The limits of the excavations to the north and east respectively are the modern streets of Vico di Mare and Vico Ferrara. It is here only that any portion of ancient Herculaneum may be seen in the open day."<ref name="Barker"/>

It is uncertain how many papyri were originally found as many of the scrolls were destroyed by workmen or when scholars extracted them from the volcanic [[tuff]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/magazine-25106956|title=Unlocking the scrolls of Herculaneum|last=Banerji|first=Robin|date=20 Dec 2013|website=BBC News|publisher=British Broadcasting Company|access-date=5 Jan 2017}}</ref>

The official list amounts to 1,814 rolls and fragments, of which 1,756 had been discovered by 1855. In the 90s it was reported that the inventory now comprises 1,826 papyri,<ref>{{cite journal | url=http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.2041-5370.1986.tb01374.x/abstract | doi=10.1111/j.2041-5370.1986.tb01374.x | title=Iv. The Herculaneum Papyri | journal=Bulletin of the Institute of Classical Studies | date=1986 | volume=33 | pages=36–45 | url-access=subscription }}</ref> with more than 340 are almost complete, about 970 are partly decayed and partly decipherable, and more than 500 are merely charred fragments.<ref name=diringer />

In a 2016 open letter, academics asked the Italian authorities to consider new excavations, since it is assumed that many more papyri may be buried at the site. Authors argue that "the volcano may erupt again and put the villa effectively beyond reach" and "Posterity will not forgive us if we squander this chance. The excavation must proceed."<ref>{{cite web |title=Further exploration at Herculaneum could 'stagger the imagination' |url=https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2016/05/19/further-exploration-at-herculaneum-could-stagger-the-imagination |website=The Art Newspaper - International art news and events |access-date=14 May 2022 |date=18 May 2016}}</ref>

In April 2024, a papyrologist at the [[University of Pisa]] found information about [[Plato]]'s burial place in the Herculaneum papyri by the usage of infrared and X-ray scanners.<ref name="smithsonian-20240501">{{Cite web |last=Anderson |first=Sonja |title=This Newly Deciphered Papyrus Scroll Reveals the Location of Plato's Grave |url=https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/platos-elusive-grave-located-after-bionic-eye-penetrates-2000-year-old-papyrus-180984221/ |website=Smithsonian Magazine |date=1 May 2024 |access-date=3 May 2024}}</ref>

===Post-excavation history===
In 1802, King [[Ferdinand IV of Naples]] offered six rolls to [[Napoleon Bonaparte]] in a diplomatic move. In 1803, along with other treasures, the scrolls were transported by [[Francesco Carelli]]. Upon receiving the gift, Bonaparte then gave the scrolls to [[Institut de France]] under charge of [[Gaspard Monge]] and [[Vivant Denon]].<ref name="napoleon1"/>

In 1810, eighteen unrolled papyri were given to [[George IV]], four of which he presented to the [[Bodleian Library]]; the rest are now mainly in the [[British Library]].<ref name=diringer/>

==Unrolling==
[[File:Tesoro letterario di Ercolano p27.jpg|thumb|Carbonized paper, found with other images in an 1858 published book by Giacomo Castrucci<ref name="GG1856">{{cite book|url=https://archive.org/stream/tesoroletterario00cast#page/n27/mode/2up|author=Giacomo Castrucci|year=1858|title=Tesoro letterario di Ercolano, ossia, La reale officina dei papiri ercolanesi|publisher=Napoli : Fibreno}}</ref>]]
Since their discovery, previous attempts used [[rose water]], liquid mercury, vegetable gas, sulfuric compounds, papyrus juice, or a mixture of ethanol, glycerin, and warm water, in hopes to make scrolls readable.<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2015/11/16/the-invisible-library|title=The Invisible Library|year=2015|magazine=The New Yorker}}</ref> According to Antonio de Simone and [[Richard Janko]], at first the papyri were mistaken for carbonized tree branches, some perhaps even thrown away or burnt to make heat.<ref name="PBS">{{cite web|title=Out of the Ashes - Recovering the Lost Library of the Herculaneum|url=http://www.kqed.org/tv/programs/archive/index.jsp?pgmid=12418&date=20050301|year=2004|publisher=PBS}}</ref>

{{rquote|right|''What we see is that the ink, which was essentially carbon based, is not very different from the carbonised papyrus.''|Dr. Vito Mocella<ref name="Webb">Jonathan Webb [https://www.bbc.com/news/science-environment-30888767 X-ray technique reads burnt Vesuvius scroll] BBC News, ''Science &amp; Environment'', 20 January 2015</ref>}}

Opening a scroll would often damage or destroy the scroll completely. If a scroll had been successfully opened, the original ink{{snd}}exposed to air{{snd}}would begin to fade. In addition, this form of unrolling often would leave pages stuck together, omitting or destroying additional information.<ref name="smithsonianmag.com"/>

With X-ray [[Micro computed tomography|micro-computed tomography]] (micro-CT), no ink can be seen, as carbon-based ink is not visible on carbonized papyrus.<ref name="smithsonianmag.com"/>

===Physical unrolling===

====Early attempts====
[[File:Abbot Piaggios machine Device-to-unroll-papyri 1756 Vatican.jpg|thumb|Abbot Piaggio's machine was used to unroll scrolls as early as 1756 in the Vatican Library.]]
Following the discovery of the Herculaneum papyri in 1752, following the advice of [[Bernardo Tanucci]], King Charles VII of Naples established a commission to study them.<ref name="Koekoe2017">{{cite web|url=http://etc.ancient.eu/education/villa-papyri/|title=Herculaneum: Villa of the Papyri|year=2017|access-date=January 19, 2019|author=Jade Koekoe}}</ref>

Possibly the first attempts to read the scrolls were made by the artist [[Camillo Paderni]] who was in charge of recovered items. Paderni used the method of slicing scrolls in half, copying readable text, by removing papyri layers. This transcription procedure was used for hundreds of scrolls, and in the process destroyed them.<ref name="Marchant2018">{{cite web|url=https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/buried-ash-vesuvius-scrolls-are-being-read-new-xray-technique-180969358/|title=Buried by the Ash of Vesuvius, These Scrolls Are Being Read for the First Time in Millennia|work=Smithsonian Magazine|author=Jo Marchant|year=2018|access-date=January 19, 2019}}</ref>

In 1756, Abbot Piaggio, conserver of ancient manuscripts in the [[Vatican Library]], used a machine he also invented,<ref name="GG1856" /> to unroll the first scroll, which took four years (millimeters per day).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://thephraser.com/2015/03/30/herculaneum-papyri-in-the-national-library-in-naples|year=2015|title=Herculaneum Papyri in the National Library in Naples|work=The Phraser|access-date=17 October 2017|archive-date=18 October 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171018071946/https://thephraser.com/2015/03/30/herculaneum-papyri-in-the-national-library-in-naples/|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="PBS"/> The results were then copied (since the writing disappeared: see above), reviewed by [[Hellenist]] academics, and then corrected once more, if necessary, by the unrolling/copying team.<ref name="napoleon1"/>

In 1802, King [[Ferdinand IV of Naples]] appointed Rev. [[John Hayter (antiquary)|John Hayter]] to assist the process.<ref name="napoleon1"/>

From 1802 to 1806, Hayter unrolled and partly deciphered some 200 papyri.<ref name=diringer /> These copies are held in the [[Bodleian Library]], where they are known as the "Oxford Facsimiles of the Herculaneum Papyri".<ref name="napoleon1"/>

In January 1816, Pierre-Claude Molard and [[Raoul Rochette]] led an attempt to unroll one papyrus with a replica of Abbot Piaggio's machine. However, the entire scroll was destroyed without any information being obtained.<ref name="napoleon1"/>

From 1819 until 1820, [[Humphry Davy]] was commissioned by the [[prince regent]] [[George IV of the United Kingdom|George IV]] to work on the Herculaneum papyri. Although it is considered that he had only limited success, Davy's chemical method, which used chlorine, managed to partially unroll 23 manuscripts.<ref>Page 203 of {{cite journal|last1=Davy|first1=Humphry|title=Some Observations and Experiments on the Papyri Found in the Ruins of Herculaneum|journal=Philosophical Transactions|date=1821|volume=111|pages=191–208|doi=10.1098/rstl.1821.0016|doi-access=free|bibcode=1821RSPT..111..191D}}</ref>

In 1877, a papyrus was taken to a laboratory in the [[Louvre]]. An attempt to unravel it was made with a "small mill", but it was unsuccessful and was mostly destroyed, leaving only a quarter intact.<ref name="napoleon1"/>

By the middle of the 20th century, only 585 rolls or fragments had been completely unrolled, and 209 unrolled in part. Of the unrolled papyri, about 200 had been deciphered and published, and about 150 only deciphered.<ref name=diringer/>

{{Multiple image
| image1            = Heruclaneum Papyrus 1521 f001r, British Library 01.jpg
| image2            = Heruclaneum Papyrus 1521 f002r, British Library.jpg
| align             = center
| total_width       = 650px

The seven fragments, recovered and published in Piaggio's workshop in Italy, were part of a gift containing a number of scrolls that King [[Ferdinand IV of Naples]] had sent to [[George IV]] of Britain in exchange for a royal giraffe for his private zoo. The scroll contains a portion of a work by the ancient Greek philosopher [[Epicurus]] (341–270 BC).<ref>{{cite web |publisher=British Library |url=https://www.bl.uk/collection-items/charred-scroll-fragments-from-herculaneum |title=Charred scroll fragments from Herculaneum |access-date=7 May 2023 |archive-date=21 August 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230821044259/https://www.bl.uk/collection-items/charred-scroll-fragments-from-herculaneum }}</ref>
}}

====Modern attempts====
{{Multiple images
| total_width = 340
| perrow      = 2
| image1      = Herculaneum papyrus 1425.png
| caption1    = Herculaneum papyrus 1425 (''De poem''), drawn by Giuseppe Casanova, {{circa|1807}}
| image2      = Herculanean Rolls - Papyrus 157-152.png
| caption2    = A copy of identifiable text of papyrus 152–157
}}

The bulk of the preserved manuscripts are housed in the Office of Herculaneum papyri in [[Biblioteca Nazionale Vittorio Emanuele III|National Library of Naples]].<ref>{{cite book |author = Marino Zorzi |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=APtYCwAAQBAJ&pg=PA478 |title= National Libraries of Italy. National Library of Naples |edition= International Dictionary of Library Histories |year= 2001 |publisher= Routledge |page = 478  |isbn = 978-1-136-77785-1 |ref= Zorzi }}</ref>

In 1969, [[Marcello Gigante]] founded the creation of the International Center for the Study of the Herculaneum Papyri (''Centro Internazionale per lo Studio dei Papiri Ercolanesi''; CISPE).<ref name="CISPE">[http://www.cispe.org/en/ CISPE] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150721153651/http://www.cispe.org/en/ |date=2015-07-21 }} ''Il Centro Internazionale per lo Studio dei Papiri Ercolanesi''</ref> With the intention of working toward the resumption of the excavation of the [[Villa of the Papyri]], and promoting the renewal of studies of the Herculaneum texts, the institution began a new method of unrolling. Using the 'Oslo' peeling method, the CISPE team separated individual layers of the papyri. One of the scrolls exploded into 300 parts, and another did similarly but to a lesser extent.<ref name="napoleon1"/>

Since 1999, the unrolled papyri have been digitized at [[Brigham Young University]] by applying [[multi-spectral image|multi-spectral imaging]] (MSI). International experts and prominent scholars participated in the project. On 4 June 2011 it was announced the task of digitizing 1,600 Herculaneum papyri had been completed.<ref>{{Cite journal |date=January 2002 |title=Digitization of Herculaneum Papyri Completed |url=https://scholarsarchive.byu.edu/insights/vol22/iss6/1/ |journal=Insights: The Newsletter of the Neal A. Maxwell Institute for Religious Scholarship |volume=22 |issue=6 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130701184553/http://maxwellinstitute.byu.edu/publications/insights/?vol=22&num=6&id=246 |archive-date=1 July 2013}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |date=January 2010 |title=BYU Herculaneum Project Honored with Mommsen Prize |url=https://scholarsarchive.byu.edu/insights/vol30/iss1/2 |journal=Insights: The Newsletter of the Neal A. Maxwell Institute for Religious Scholarship |volume=30 |issue=1 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130701184122/http://maxwellinstitute.byu.edu/publications/insights/?vol=30&num=1&id=894 |archive-date=1 July 2013}}</ref> MSI helps spot ink because the ink and the charred papyrus have different reflectivities in the 950 nm infrared band. The images are not actually "multispectral", but consist only of data in this 950-nm band.<ref name=pmid31620553>{{cite journal |last1=Tournié |first1=A |last2=Fleischer |first2=K |last3=Bukreeva |first3=I |last4=Palermo |first4=F |last5=Perino |first5=M |last6=Cedola |first6=A |last7=Andraud |first7=C |last8=Ranocchia |first8=G |title=Ancient Greek text concealed on the back of unrolled papyrus revealed through shortwave-infrared hyperspectral imaging. |journal=Science Advances |date=October 2019 |volume=5 |issue=10 |article-number=eaav8936 |doi=10.1126/sciadv.aav8936 |pmid=31620553 |pmc=6777967|bibcode=2019SciA....5.8936T }}</ref>

In 2019, a multinational European team reported that SWIR HSI ([[Short-wave infrared|shortwave-infrared]] [[hyperspectral imaging]]), which combines several bands in the 1000–2500 nm range, detects ink on unrolled papyri better than the 950 nm technique does.<ref name=pmid31620553/>

===Virtual unrolling===
Several research groups have proposed to unroll the scrolls virtually, using [[X-ray Phase Contrast Tomography|X-ray phase-contrast tomography]] (XPCT, "phase-contrast CT"), possibly with a [[synchrotron light source]]. The proposed method has four steps: volumetric scanning, segmentation, layered texture generation and restoration.<ref name="Bukreeva">{{cite journal |last=Bukreeva |first=I. |display-authors=etal |date=2016 |title=Virtual unrolling and deciphering of Herculaneum papyri by X-ray phase-contrast tomography |url= |journal=Scientific Reports |volume=6 |article-number= 30364|doi= 10.1038/srep30364|doi-access= free|pmc= 5016987|pmid= 27608927| name-list-style=vanc|bibcode=2016NatSR...630364B}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Vergano |first=Dan |date=January 22, 2015 |title=X-Rays Reveal Snippets From Papyrus Scrolls That Survived Mount Vesuvius |url=http://news.nationalgeographic.com/news/2015/01/150120-roman-scrolls-xray-archeology-science/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150121160151/http://news.nationalgeographic.com/news/2015/01/150120-roman-scrolls-xray-archeology-science/ |archive-date=January 21, 2015 |newspaper=National Geographic }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Mocella | first1 = Vito | last2 = Brun | first2 = Emmanuel | last3 = Ferrero | first3 = Claudio | last4 = Delattre | first4 = Daniel | year = 2015 | title = Revealing letters in rolled Herculaneum papyri by X-ray phase-contrast imaging | journal = Nature Communications | volume = 6 | article-number = 5895 | doi = 10.1038/ncomms6895 | pmid = 25603114 | bibcode = 2015NatCo...6.5895M | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref name="smithsonianmag.com"/><ref>{{cite arXiv |last=Bukreeva |first=I. |display-authors=etal |date=2016 |title=Enhanced X-ray-phase-contrast-tomography brings new clarity to the 2000-year-old 'voice' of Epicurean philosopher Philodemus |eprint=1602.08071|class=physics.soc-ph }}</ref>

Since 2007, a team working with Institut de Papyrologie and a group of scientists from [[Kentucky]] have been using X-rays and [[nuclear magnetic resonance]] to analyze the artifacts.<ref name="napoleon1"/>

In 2009, the [[Institut de France]] in conjunction with the [[French National Centre for Scientific Research]] imaged two intact Herculaneum papyri using X-ray micro-computed tomography (micro-CT) to reveal the interior structures of the scrolls.<ref>{{cite AV media | type=Video | year=2011 | title=EDUCE: Imaging the Herculaneum Scrolls | url=https://vimeo.com/22606936 |publisher=Center for Visualization & Virtual Environments, U. Kentucky }}</ref><ref>W. Brent Seales, James Griffioen, Ryan Baumann, Matthew Field (2011) [http://www.ndt.net/article/art2011/papers/FIELD%20-%20M%2014.pdf ANALYSIS OF HERCULANEUM PAPYRI WITH X-RAY COMPUTED TOMOGRAPHY] Center for Visualization &amp; Virtual Environments; U. Kentucky</ref> The team heading the project estimated that if the scrolls were fully unwound they would be between {{convert|11|and|15|m}} long.<ref name="smithsonianmag.com"/> The internal structure of the rolls was revealed to be too compact and convoluted for the automated algorithms the team had developed. Unfortunately, no ink could be seen on the small samples imaged, because carbon-based inks are not visible on the carbonized scrolls.<ref name="smithsonianmag.com"/> However, some scrolls were written with ink containing lead.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Revealing metallic ink in Herculaneum papyri|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|volume=113|issue=14|pages=3751–3754|doi=10.1073/pnas.1519958113|pmid=27001841|pmc=4833268|author=Brun|display-authors=etal|year=2016|bibcode=2016PNAS..113.3751B|doi-access=free}}</ref>

In September 2016, Brent Seales, Professor, Department of Computer Science at the [[University of Kentucky]], successfully used virtual unrolling to read the text of a charred parchment from Israel, the [[En-Gedi Scroll]].<ref name="EnGedi">{{Cite news | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/09/22/science/ancient-sea-scrolls-bible.html |title = Modern Technology Unlocks Secrets of a Damaged Biblical Scroll|newspaper = The New York Times|date = 21 September 2016|last1 = Wade|first1 = Nicholas}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Seales |first1=William Brent |last2=Parker |first2=Clifford Seth |last3=Segal |first3=Michael |last4=Tov |first4=Emanuel |last5=Shor |first5=Pnina |last6=Porath |first6=Yosef |title=From damage to discovery via virtual unwrapping: Reading the scroll from En-Gedi |journal=Science Advances |date=2 September 2016 |volume=2 |issue=9 |article-number=e1601247 |doi=10.1126/sciadv.1601247 |pmid=27679821 |pmc=5031465 |bibcode=2016SciA....2E1247S }}</ref>

====Process====
{{Main|Virtual unfolding}}
The virtual unrolling process begins with a volumetric scan of the damaged scroll. Such scans are non-invasive, and generate a virtual 3D model of the scroll in which ink can be distinguished from paper. After the scan, the unrolling process consists only of manipulation of the data so obtained, so the scroll is returned to the archive. This also affords researchers the flexibility to select for scanning methods which yield the greatest contrast between ink and paper and to quickly adapt to improved scanning methods as they develop. In the case of the Herculaneum papyri, the volumetric scan used [[Phase-contrast X-ray imaging|phase-contrast CT]].<ref name="Bukreeva"/> 

The Herculaneum papyri were written using a carbon-based ink, the chemical composition of which is extremely similar to that of the surrounding carbonized parchment. This poses an obstacle to standard imaging techniques like [[CT scan|CT scanning]], which distinguish parts of an object according to their [[absorption (electromagnetic radiation)|absorption]] and [[Emission spectrum|emission]] properties. However, the presence of ink at a particular point on the parchment results in the scroll being slightly thicker at that point than in its immediate vicinity. Consequently, suitability of a scanning technique for unrolling of the Herculaneum papyri depends largely on its ability to resolve this difference. Phase-contrast CT accomplishes this because radiation passing through a material will undergo a [[Phase (waves)|phase]] shift which depends on the material's thickness;<ref name="ndt-2008" /> however, [[X-ray microtomography|micro-CT]] is also considered a suitable technique by virtue of its sheer resolution.<ref name="ndt-2008">{{cite conference |last1=Baumann |first1=Ryan |last2=Porter |first2=Dorothy |last3=Seales |first3=W. |title=The use of micro-CT in the study of archaeological artifacts |conference=9th International Conference on NDT of Art |year=2008 |location=Jerusalem}}</ref> 
 
The virtual model produced by the scan records the composition of the scroll at an array of small regions in space called [[voxel]]s or volume-pixels. The goal from this point is to construct a two-dimensional representation of the unrolled scroll in such a way that the voxels corresponding to points on the rolled-up scroll can be identified with corresponding pixels on the constructed unrolling. This process happens in three steps: segmentation, texturing and flattening.

In 2018, Seales demonstrated a readable virtual unrolling of parts of a Herculaneum papyrus (P.Herc. 118) from the [[Bodleian Library]], at [[Oxford University]], which was given by King Ferdinand of Naples to the Prince of Wales in 1810. The imaging method Seales used involved a handheld scanner called an Artec Space Spider.<ref name=Marchant2018/> In the same year, he demonstrated a readable unrolling of another Herculaneum scroll, with help of the [[particle accelerator]] [[Diamond Light Source]]; through an X-ray imaging technique, ink containing trace amounts of lead was detected.<ref name=Marchant2018/> Prior to this, he demonstrated a successful virtual unrolling without detecting ink on Herculaneum scrolls.<ref>{{cite conference|conference=International Conference on nondestructive investigations and microanalysis for the diagnostics and conservation of cultural and environmental heritage|url=https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/2d1a/8f2a807a91f0a5bb6e10051f2c7f0432059a.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190120044516/https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/2d1a/8f2a807a91f0a5bb6e10051f2c7f0432059a.pdf|archive-date=2019-01-20|title=Analysis Of Herculaneum Papyri With X-ray Computed Tomography|author=W. Brent Seales|year=2011|s2cid=7667891}}</ref>

====Vesuvius Challenge====
In 2023, [[Nat Friedman]], [[Daniel Gross (entrepreneur)|Daniel Gross]], and computer scientist [[Brent Seales]] announced the Vesuvius Challenge, a competition to "decipher Herculaneum scrolls using 3D X-ray software".<ref>{{cite web |title=Vesuvius Challenge |url=https://scrollprize.org/ |access-date=17 March 2023 |website=scrollprize.org |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Sample |first1=Ian |date=15 March 2023 |title=Contest launched to decipher Herculaneum scrolls using 3D X-ray software |url=https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2023/mar/15/contest-decipher-herculaneum-scrolls-3d-x-ray-software |access-date=17 March 2023 |website=The Guardian}}</ref> The Vesuvius Challenge offered a $700,000 grand prize to be awarded to the first team that could extract four passages of text from two intact scrolls using 3D X-ray scans.<ref>{{Cite web |title=$700,000 grand prize (December 31st) |url=https://scrollprize.org/grand_prize |access-date=13 October 2023 |website=scrollprize.org |publisher=Vesuvius Challenge}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Parker |first=Christopher |date=24 March 2023 |title=You Could Win $1 Million by Deciphering These Ancient Roman Scrolls |work=[[Smithsonian (magazine)|Smithsonian Magazine]] |url=https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/over-1m-up-for-grabs-if-you-can-unlock-the-secrets-of-these-roman-scrolls-from-pompeii-180981867/ |access-date=13 October 2023}}</ref> 

On 12 October 2023, the project awarded $40,000 to [[Luke Farritor]], a 21-year-old computer science student at the University of Nebraska, for successfully detecting the first word in an unopened scroll: ''porphyras'' ({{langx|grc|[[wikt:πορφύρα|ΠΟΡΦΥΡΑϹ]]| |purple|link=no}}).<ref>{{Cite web |date=12 October 2023 |title=First word discovered in unopened Herculaneum scroll by 21yo computer science student |url=https://scrollprize.org/firstletters |access-date=13 October 2023 |website=scrollprize.org |publisher=Vesuvius Challenge}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Wade |first=Nicholas |author-link=Nicholas Wade |date=12 October 2023 |title=Scrolls That Survived Vesuvius Divulge Their First Word |work=[[The New York Times]] |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2023/10/12/arts/design/herculaneum-scroll-vesuvius-word-purple.html |access-date=13 October 2023}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Sample |first=Ian |date=12 October 2023 |title=Researchers use AI to read word on ancient scroll burned by Vesuvius |work=The Guardian |url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2023/oct/12/researchers-use-ai-to-read-word-on-ancient-scroll-burned-by-vesuvius |access-date=13 October 2023}}</ref> With this milestone "first word" award included, the project has awarded $260,000 in total for segmentation tooling and ink detection (from segmented volumes).<ref>{{cite web |title=Prize Winners |url=https://scrollprize.org/winners |website=Vesuvius Challenge |access-date=13 October 2023 |language=en}}</ref>

On 5 February 2024, the project awarded its 2023 Grand Prize of $700,000 to the winning team and $50,000 each to three runner-up teams for successfully revealing 5% of [[PHerc. Paris. 4|one scroll]], and announced its goal for 2024 of revealing 90% of the four scrolls that it has fully scanned.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://scrollprize.org/grandprize |title=Vesuvius Challenge 2023 Grand Prize awarded: we can read the first scroll! |website=Vesuvius Challenge |date=5 February 2024 |language=en |access-date=5 February 2024 |quote=Of the remaining submissions, the scores from our team of papyrologists identify a three-way tie for runner up.}}</ref> The uncovered text is believed to be a previously unknown text of [[Philodemus]], "centered on the pleasures of music and food and their effects on the senses".<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Marchant |first=Jo |date=2024-02-05 |title=First passages of rolled-up Herculaneum scroll revealed |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-024-00346-8 |journal=Nature |volume=626 |issue=7999 |pages=461–462 |doi=10.1038/d41586-024-00346-8|pmid=38316998 |bibcode=2024Natur.626..461M |s2cid=267497364 |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

In 2025, the scans of the scrolls that were provided to participants in the Vesuvius Challenge for the purpose of fully reading them are Scroll 1 ([[PHerc. Paris. 4]]), from the Institut de France, which is 5% read, Scroll 2 (PHerc. Paris 3), from the Institut de France, Scroll 3 (PHerc. 332), from the Biblioteca Nazionale di Napoli, a smaller scroll known as the midollo (marrow), left over from attempts to physically unroll the larger original scroll, Scroll 4 (PHerc. 1667), from the Biblioteca Nazionale di Napoli, similar in size to Scroll 3, and Scroll 5 (PHerc. 172), from the Bodleian Library in Oxford, similar in size to Scroll 1.<ref>{{cite web | title=Vesuvius Challenge | url=https://scrollprize.org/data_scrolls }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | title=Vesuvius Challenge | url=https://scrollprize.org/grand_prize }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | title=Vesuvius Challenge | url=https://scrollprize.org/data }}</ref>

In June 2026, the Vesuvius Challenge team announced that PHerc. 1667, known within the project as "Scroll 4", had been virtually unwrapped and read end-to-end.<ref name="CISPEpress2026">{{cite web |title=PRESS EVENT – 25th JUNE 2026 |url=https://cispe.org/en/press-event-25th-june-2026/ |website=CISPE Marcello Gigante |publisher=Centro Internazionale per lo Studio dei Papiri Ercolanesi |date=9 June 2026 |access-date=2 July 2026}}</ref><ref name="Reuters2026">{{cite news |last=Balmer |first=Crispian |title=Complete text of carbonised Herculaneum scroll unlocked for first time |url=https://www.reuters.com/science/complete-text-carbonised-herculaneum-scroll-unlocked-first-time-2026-06-25/ |work=Reuters |date=25 June 2026 |access-date=2 July 2026}}</ref><ref name="FirstScroll">{{cite web |title=We read an entire scroll — without ever opening it |url=https://scrollprize.org/firstscroll |website=Vesuvius Challenge |date=25 June 2026 |access-date=2 July 2026}}</ref> A project preprint described the work as the first complete virtual unwrapping and extended reading of a rolled Herculaneum papyrus. In the PHerc. 1667, 22 columns of text were recovered, containing "a [[Stoic]] philosophical treatise that may be attributable to [[Chrysippus]]".<ref>{{cite web |last=Scott |first=Anastasia |title=A Herculaneum Scroll Is Readable Again Nearly 2,000 Years After Vesuvius Buried It |website=Discover Magazine |date=2026-06-29 |url=https://www.discovermagazine.com/a-herculaneum-scroll-is-readable-again-nearly-2-000-years-after-vesuvius-buried-it-49306 |access-date=2026-07-03}}</ref> Besides PHerc. 1667, the team were able to read the title and author of PHerc. 139: [[Philodemus]], ''On Gods, Book 8''.<ref name="Angelotti2026"/>

==Significance==
[[Image:Tetrapharmakos PHerc 1005 col 5.png|thumb|A papyrus copy depicting the Epicurean [[tetrapharmakos]] in Philodemus' ''Adversus Sophistas''&nbsp;– (P.Herc.1005), col. 5]]
Until the middle of the 18th century, the only papyri known were a few survivals from medieval times.<ref>[[Frederic G. Kenyon]], [https://archive.org/stream/cu31924024493649#page/n13/mode/2up ''Palaeography of Greek papyri''] (Oxford, Clarendon Press, 1899), p. 3.</ref> Most likely, these rolls never would have survived the [[Mediterranean climate]] and would have crumbled or been lost. Indeed, all these rolls have come from the only surviving library from antiquity that exists in its entirety.<ref name="napoleon1"/>

These papyri contain a large number of [[Greek Philosophy|Greek philosophical texts]]. Large parts of Books XIV, XV, XXV, and XXVIII of the magnum opus of [[Epicurus]], ''[[On Nature (Epicurus)|On Nature]]'' and works by early followers of Epicurus are also represented among the papyri.<ref name=CISPE /> Of the rolls, 44{{citation needed|date=September 2015}} have been identified as the work of [[Philodemus of Gadara]], an [[Epicureanism|Epicurean]] philosopher and poet. The manuscript "PHerc.Paris.2" contains part of Philodemus' ''On Vices and Virtues''.<ref name="napoleon1"/>

The [[Stoicism|Stoic]] philosopher [[Chrysippus]] is attested to have written over 700 works,<ref>[[Diogenes Laërtius]], ''[[Lives and Opinions of Eminent Philosophers]]'', vii. 180</ref> all of them lost, with the exception of a few fragments quoted by other authors.<ref name="sellars8">John Sellars, ''Stoicism''. University of California Press, 2007. - p. 8</ref> Segments of his works ''On Providence'' and ''Logical Questions'' were found among the papyri;<ref name="sellars8"/> a third work of his may have been recovered from the charred rolls.<ref name="fitzgerald">{{cite book |last=Fitzgerald |first=John T. |year=2004 |contribution=Philodemus and the Papyri from Herculaneum |editor-last=Fitzgerald |editor-first=John T. |editor2-last=Obbink |editor2-first=Dirk |editor3-last=Holland |editor3-first=Glenn Stanfield |title=Philodemus and the New Testament world Philosophy |publisher=Brill |isbn=90-04-11460-2 |page=11 |quote=The first of Chrysippus' partially preserved two or three works is his ''Logical Questions'', contained in PHerc. 307 ... The second work is his ''On Providence'', preserved in PHerc 1038 and 1421 ... A third work, most likely by Chrysippus is preserved in PHerc. 1020,}}</ref>

Parts of a poem on the [[Battle of Actium]] have also survived in the library.<ref>Gregory Hays, [https://www.the-tls.co.uk/articles/keeping-things-platonic/ "Keeping Things Platonic: A new discovery of a possible lost book by Apuleius on Plato"] [review of Justin A Stover, ''A New Work by Apuleius''], ''Times Literary Supplement'' 20 May 2016 p. 29. {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200920024830/https://www.the-tls.co.uk/articles/keeping-things-platonic/|date=2020-09-20}}.</ref>

In May 2018, it was reported that fragments of the lost work ''Histories'' by [[Seneca the Elder]] had been found on a papyrus scroll (PHerc. 1067).<ref>{{cite web | first = Carlo | last = Marino | date = 21 May 2018 | title = Lucius Anneus Seneca the Elder's Histories | publisher = European News Agency | url = https://www.european-news-agency.de/kunst_kultur_und_musik/lucius_anneus_seneca_the_elders_histories_-71128/ | access-date = 21 September 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190525011539/https://www.european-news-agency.de/kunst_kultur_und_musik/lucius_anneus_seneca_the_elders_histories_-71128/ |archive-date=25 May 2019 }}</ref>

In February 2023, classical scholar [[Richard Janko]] announced that he and Seales' team, assisted by [[artificial intelligence]], had managed to read a small part of one heavily damaged, previously unreadable Herculaneum papyrus. The text appeared to be part of a [[Historiography of Alexander the Great|lost work about]] [[Alexander the Great]] and the [[Diadochi]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.livescience.com/ai-is-deciphering-a-2000-year-old-lost-book-describing-life-after-alexander-the-great|title=AI is deciphering a 2,000-year-old 'lost book' describing life after Alexander the Great|author1=Owen Jarus|date=7 February 2023|website=livescience.com|access-date=10 January 2024}}</ref>

In April 2024, the research of a papyrologist at the [[University of Pisa]] uncovered details about [[Plato]]'s burial site from the Herculaneum papyri using [[infrared]] and [[X-ray]] scanning techniques. This research revealed that Plato's tomb was situated within a garden designated for him at the Platonic school, close to the [[Mouseion]] dedicated to the muses.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-04-25 |title=The papyri of Herculaneum reveal the location of Plato's tomb |url=https://www.lavanguardia.com/mediterranean/20240425/9603140/papyrus-herculaneum-plato-tomb-vesuvius-athens-academy.html |access-date=2024-05-03 |website=La Vanguardia |language=en}}</ref><ref name="smithsonian-20240501" />
